stem_md:
Prove that the determinant of the matrix   $$ \begin{pmatrix}
a_{1}^{2}+k & a_1 a_2 & a_1 a_3 &\ldots & a_1 a_n
a_2 a_1 & a_{2}^{2}+k & a_2 a_3 &\ldots & a_2 a_n
\ldots & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots 
a_n a_1& a_n a_2 & a_n a_3 & \ldots & a_{n}^{2}+k
\end{pmatrix} $$  is divisible by  $k^{n-1}$  and find its other factor.
solution_md:
Let  $A= - \begin{pmatrix}
a_{1}^{2} & a_1 a_2 & a_1 a_3 &\ldots & a_1 a_n
a_2 a_1 & a_{2}^{2} & a_2 a_3 &\ldots & a_2 a_n
\ldots & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots 
a_n a_1& a_n a_2 & a_n a_3 & \ldots & a_{n}^{2}
\end{pmatrix}$ Then the given matrix is the characteristic polynomial of A. 

(denote by  $\phi_A (k)$ )

Since  $rank(A)$  is 0  $($ iff  $(a_1,a_2,\ldots, a_n) = (0,0,,\ldots, 0))$  or 1 $($ iff  $(a_1,a_2,\ldots, a_n) \neq (0,0,,\ldots, 0))$ , 0 is an eigenvalue of  $A$  and also,  $geo(0) \ge n-1$ .
Applying  $alg(0) \ge geo(0)$ , we get  $\phi_A (k) = k^{n-1}(k-\alpha)$ .

Now, by using the fact that the sum of all eigenvalues is equal to the trace of the matrix, we conclude  $\alpha = -(a_1^2 + a_2^2 + \cdots + a_n^2)$ .

stem_md: Find the  $n$ -th derivative with respect to  $x$  of  $$ \int_{0}^{x} \left(1+\frac{x-t}{1!}+\frac{(x-t)^{2}}{2!}+\ldots+\frac{(x-t)^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}\right)e^{nt} dt. $$
solution_md: Let  $S_n(x,t)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\frac{(x-t)^i}{i!}$  so that  $\int_0^x\left(1+\frac{x-t}{1!}+...+\frac{(x-t)^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}\right)e^{nt}dt=\int_0^xS_n(x,t)e^{nt}dt=f_n(x)$ . We have :  $\forall x\in\mathbb R$ ,   $$ f_n'(x)=\lim_{h\rightarrow0}\frac1h\left(\int_0^{x+h}S_n(x+h,t)e^{nt}dt-\int_0^xS_n(x,t)e^{nt}dt\right) $$    $$ =\lim_{h\rightarrow0}\left(\int_0^x\left(\frac{S_n(x+h,t)-S_n(x,t)}{h}\right)e^{nt}dt+\frac1h\int_x^{x+h}S_n(x+h,t)e^{nt}dt\right) $$    $$ =\int_0^x\frac{\partial S_n}{\partial x}(x,t)e^{nt}dt+S_n(x,x)e^{nx} $$  Since  $S_n(x,x)=1$  and  $\frac{\partial S_n}{\partial x}(x,t)=S_{n-1}(x,t)$ , we have :  $$ f_n'(x)=\int_0^xS_{n-1}(x,t)e^{nt}dt+e^{nx}=f_{n-1}(x)+e^{nx} $$  Therefore we get by induction that  $f_n^{(n)}(x)=e^{nx}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}n^i$

stem_md: A circle of radius  $a$  rolls in the plane along the  $x$ -axis. Show that the envelope of a diameter is a cycloid, coinciding with the cycloid traced out by a point on the circumference of a circle of diameter  $a$ , likewise rolling in the plane along the  $x$ -axis.
solution_md:
I post both solution;**First solution:** Let two circles roll along the upper side of  $x-$ axis so that at time  $t$  they both touch the axis at  $(at, 0).$  Let  $P$  and  $Q$  be the points that start in contact with the origin  $O,$  and let  $D$  and  $E$  be the center of the larger and smaller circles, respectively. Let  $P'$  be the point opposite  $P$  on the larger circle. We may suppose that  $PP'$  is the moving diameter of the problem, since we can choose the origin along  $x-$ axis at our convenience. The point  $Q$  traces a cycloid  $C,$  and we shall prove that  $PP'$  is always tangent to  $C$  at  $Q.$  This will prove that the envelope of  $PP'$  is  $C.$  Since  $\overarc {PT}=\overarc {QT}=OT=at,$  while the circles are of radius  $a$  and  $\frac{a}{2},$  we see that  $\angle PDT=t,$   $\angle QET=2t.$  Hence at time  $t,$   $P$  is at so that the tangent to  $C$  at  $Q$  has the representation:  $$ x=at-\frac{a}{2}sin\ 2t+u(a-a\ cos\ 2t) $$   $(1)$   $$ y=\frac{a}{2}-\frac{a}{2}cos\ 2t+u(a\ sin\ 2t) $$  in terms of the parameter  $u.$  Putting:  $$ u=\frac{cos\ t-1}{2\ sin\ t} \ \text{and} \ u=\frac{cos\ t+1}{2\ sin\ t} $$  in  $(1),$  we see that  $P$  and  $P'$  are both on the tangent line. This proves  $PP'$  is tangent to  $C$  at  $Q$  for  $t$  not a multiple of  $\pi.$  When  $t$  is a multiple of  $\pi,$   $Q$  is on the  $x-$ axis, the curve  $C$  has a cusp at  $Q$  with a vertical tangent, and  $PP'$  is tangent to  $C$  in this case too.**Second Solution:** A purely synthetic can be given as follows:

stem_md: Let the roots  $a,b,c$  of   $$ f(x)=x^3 +p x^2 + qx+r $$  be real, and let  $a\leq b\leq c$ . Prove that  $f'(x)$  has a root in the interval  $\left[\frac{b+c}{2}, \frac{b+2c}{3}\right]$ . What will be the form of  $f(x)$  if the root in question falls at either end of the interval?
solution_md: The proposition is vali for  $f(x)$  iff it is valid for  $f(x+b$  so we can translate all the roots by  $-b$  and thus arrange that the middle root is zero. It is no loss of generality, therefore, to assume that  $b=0$  to begin with. Hence we consider:  $$ f(x)=x (x-a)(x-c)=x^3-(a+c)x^2+acx $$  where  $a \le 0 \le c.$  The fourth subinterval referred to in the problem is  $[\frac{c}{2}, \frac{2c}{3}].$  From  $f'(x)= 3x^2-2(a+c)x+ac$  we find  $f'(\frac{c}{2}=-\frac{1}{4}c^2\le 0$  and  $f'(\frac{2c}{3}=-\frac{-1}{3}ac \ge 0.$  Hence, since  $f'$  is continuous, there is a root of  $f'(x)=0$  on  $[\frac{c}{2}, \frac{2c}{3}].$  A root occurs at the left endpoint  $\frac{c}{2}$  iff  $c=0;$  That is, the two largest roots coincide. In this event,  $f(x)=x^2(x-a).$  A root occurs at the right endpoint  $\frac{2c}{3}$  iff  $a=0$  or  $c=0.$  If  $c=0$  we have the previous case, and the interval in question has degenerated to single point. If  $c \not= 0,$  then  $a=0$  and the two smallest roots coincide. To answer the second part of the question in terms of the original,  $a, b, c:$ The zero of  $f'$  occurs at the left endpoint iff  $f(x)=(x-a)(x-b)^2$  and at the right endpoint iff  $f(x)=(x-b)^2(x-c)$  or  $f(x)=(x-a)(x-b)^2.$

stem_md: A particle  $(x,y)$  moves so that its angular velocities about  $(1,0)$  and  $(-1,0)$  are equal in magnitude but opposite in sign. Prove that  $$ y(x^2 +y^2 +1)\; dx= x(x^2 +y^2 -1) \;dy, $$  and verify that this is the differential equation of the family of rectangular hyperbolas passing through  $(1,0)$  and  $(-1,0)$  and having the origin as center.
solution_md:
The angular momentum (for unit mass) about  $(1, 0)$  is  $(x - 1) dy/dt - y dx/dt$ . Hence the angular velocity is  $\frac{(x - 1) dy/dt - y dx/dt}{(x - 1)^2 + y^2}$ . Similarly, the angular velocity about  $(-1, 0)$  is  $\frac{(x + 1) dy/dt - y dx/dt}{(x + 1)^2 + y^2}$ . Hence the trajectory satisfies:  $[(x - 1)y' - y](x^2 + y^2 + 1 + 2x) + [(x + 1)y' - y](x^2 + y^2 + 1 - 2x) = 0$ , or  $2xy'(x^2 + y^2 + 1) - 4xy' - 2y(x^2 + y^2 + 1) = 0$ , or  $xy'(x^2 + y^2 - 1) = y(x^2 + y^2 + 1)$ .

We see immediately that  $xy = 0$  is a solution and almost immediately that  $x^2 - y^2 = 1$  is a solution. Hence, so are all linear combinations  $x^2 + k xy - y^2 = 1$ . These are rectangular hyperbolae because the sum of the coefficients of  $x^2$  and  $y^2$  are zero.

stem_md:
Find 
(i)  $\lim_{n\to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{\sqrt{n^2 +i^{2}}}$ .
(ii)  $\lim_{n\to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{\sqrt{n^2 +i}}$ .
(iii)  $\lim_{n\to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^{n^{2}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{n^2 +i}}$ .
solution_md:
(i) just reimann summation

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>$$ \lim_{n\to \infty}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n^2 +i^{2}}}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+(\frac{i}{n})^2}}=\int_0^1 \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}=\ln(x+\sqrt{1+x^2})\big|_0^1=\ln(1+\sqrt{2}) $$</details>

(ii) bounding and then squeeze

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>$\frac{1}{\sqrt{n^2 +n}}\le\frac{1}{\sqrt{n^2 +i}}\le\frac{1}{\sqrt{n^2 +1}}$ now summing  $\lim_{n\to\infty}$   $\frac{n}{\sqrt{n^2 +n}}\le\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{\sqrt{n^2 +i}}\le\frac{n}{\sqrt{n^2 +1}}=1$</details>

(iii) kind of bounding maybe? <details><summary>spoiler</summary>except that isn't</details>

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>$\frac{1}{\sqrt{n^2 +i}}>\frac{1}{\sqrt{n^2 +n}}$ again summing  $\lim_{n\to\infty}$   $\sum_{i=1}^{n^{2}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{n^2 +i}}<\frac{n^2}{\sqrt{n^2 +n}}$ hence it diverges</details>

(i)  $\underset{n\to \infty }{\mathop{\lim }}\,\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{{{n}^{2}}+{{i}^{2}}}}}=\underset{n\to \infty }{\mathop{\lim }}\,\frac{1}{n}\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{{\left( \frac{i}{n} \right)}^{2}}}}}=\int\limits_{0}^{1}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{{x}^{2}}}}}=\left[ \ln (x+\sqrt{{{x}^{2}}+1} \right]_{0}^{1}=\ln \left( 1+\sqrt{2} \right)$

$\emph{Solution.}$ (i)   $\underset{n\to \infty }{\mathop{\lim }}\,\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{{{n}^{2}}+{{i}^{2}}}}}=\underset{n\to \infty }{\mathop{\lim }}\,\frac{1}{n}\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{{\left( \frac{i}{n} \right)}^{2}}}}}=\int\limits_{0}^{1}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{{x}^{2}}}}}=\left\{ \ln (x+\sqrt{{{x}^{2}}+1} )\right\}_{0}^{1}=\ln \left( 1+\sqrt{2} \right)$ (ii)  $1= \underset{n\to \infty }{\mathop{\lim }}\,\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}{\frac{n}{\sqrt{{{n}^{2}}+{{n}^{{}}}}}}\le \underset{n\to \infty }{\mathop{\lim }}\,\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{{{n}^{2}}+{{i}^{{}}}}}}\le \underset{n\to \infty }{\mathop{\lim }}\,\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}{\frac{n}{\sqrt{{{n}^{2}}+1}}}= 1$  so by squeeze theorem the limit of desired sum is also  $1$ .

(iii) there are  $n^2$  terms, each at least  $\frac{1}{n \sqrt{2}}$  so the sum is at least  $\frac{n}{\sqrt{2}}$  which diverges.

stem_md: Let  $y_1$  and  $y_2$  be two linearly independent solutions of the equation  $$ y''+P(x)y'+Q(x)=0. $$  Find the differential equation satisfied by the product  $z=y_1 y_2$ .
solution_md:
Let us take: $w = yz$ ; $w' = y'z + yz'$ ; $w'' = y''z + 2y'z' + yz''$ . 

Hence,  $w'' + pw' + 2qw = 2y'z'$  (i).  Now  $(y'z')' = y''z' + y'z'', 2py'z' = py'z' + py'z', qw' = qyz' + qy'z$ , so  $(y'z')' + 2py'z' + qw' = 0$  (ii).

Differentiating (i) yields:  $w''' + p'w' + pw'' + 2q'w + 2qw' = 2(y'z')' = -4py'z' - 2qw'$ ;

and using (ii) produces: $= -2p(w'' + pw' + 2qw) - 2qw'$ . 

Rearranging gives:  $w''' + 3p w'' + (p' + 2p2 + 4q)w' + (4pq + 2q')w = 0$ .

stem_md:
Given two perpendicular diameters  $AB$  and  $CD$  of an ellipse, we say that the diameter  $A'B'$  is conjugate to  $AB$  if  $A'B'$  is parallel to the tangent to the ellipse at  $A$ . Let  $A'B'$  be conjugate to  $AB$  and  $C'D'$  be conjugate to  $CD$ .
Prove that the rectangular hyperbola through  $A', B', C'$  and  $D'$  passes through the foci of the ellipse.
solution_md:
Take the ellipse as  $x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1$  and the point  $A$  as  $(a*cos(t), b*sin(t))$ . Then  $AB$  has slope  $b/a \cdot tan(t)$ , so  $CD$  has slope  $-a/b \cdot cot(t)$ . The tangent at  $A$  has slope  $-b/a \cdot cot(t)$ . Suppose  $C$  is  $(a*cos(u), b*sin(u))$ , then  $b/a \cdot tan(u) = -a/b \cdot cot(t)$  and the tangent at  $C$  has slope  $-b/a \cdot cot(u) = b^3/a^3 \cdot tan(t)$ . Hence the line pair  $A'B', C'D'$  has equation  $[y + bx/a \cdot cot (t)][y - x \cdot b^3/a^3 tan(t)]$ . Now we have the equations for two distinct conics through  $A'B'C'D'$ : the original ellipse and the line pair  $A'B',C'D'$ . The equation of any other conic through these four points must be a linear combination of the equations of these two, in other words: $(x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 - 1) + k[y + bx/a \cdot cot(t)][y - x \cdot b^3/a^3 tan(t)] = 0$  

for some  $k$ .

The criterion for a rectangular hyperbola is that the coefficients of  $x^2$  and  $y^2$  should have sum zero, or that  $1/a^2 + 1/b^2 + k(1 - b^4/a^4) = 0$ . Hence  $k = a^2/(b^4-b^2a^2)$  and the equation of the rectangular hyperbola is  $x^2 - y^2 + [b/a \cdot tan(t) - a/b \cdot cot(t)]xy = a^2 - b^2$ . But the foci are at  $(\pm \sqrt{a^2 - b^2}, 0)$ , so they lie on the rectangular hyperbola.

stem_md: Assuming that  $f(x)$  is continuous in the interval  $(0,1)$ , prove that  $$ \int_{x=0}^{x=1} \int_{y=x}^{y=1} \int_{z=x}^{z=y} f(x)f(y)f(z)\;dz dy dx= \frac{1}{6}\left(\int_{0}^{1} f(t)\; dt\right)^{3}. $$
solution_md:
That  $dx \ dy \ dz$  should be  $dz \ dy \ dx.$  Let   $$ g(x):=\int_0^xf(t) \ dt. $$   
Then    $$ \int_0^1 \int_x^1 \int_x^y f(x)f(y)f(z) \ dz \ dy \ dx=\int_0^1 \int_x^1g'(x)g'(y)(g(y)-g(x)) \ dy \ dx $$    $$ =\int_0^1g'(x)\int_x^1g'(y)g(y) \ dy \ dx - \int_0^1g(x)g'(x) \int_x^1g'(y) \ dy \ dx $$    $$ =\frac{1}{2}\int_0^1g'(x)(g(1)^2-g(x)^2) \ dx - \int_0^1g(x)g'(x)(g(1)-g(x)) \ dx $$    $$ =\frac{1}{2}g(1)^2 \int_0^1g'(x) \ dx -\frac{1}{2}\int_0^1g'(x)g(x)^2 \ dx-g(1) \int_0^1g'(x)g(x) \ dx + \int_0^1g'(x)g(x)^2 \ dx $$    $$ =\frac{1}{2}g(1)^3-\frac{1}{6}g(1)^3-\frac{1}{2}g(1)^3+\frac{1}{3}g(1)^3=\frac{1}{6}g(1)^3=\frac{1}{6}\left(\int_0^1f(t) \ dt\right)^3. $$

stem_md:
A square of side  $2a$ , lying always in the first quadrant of the  $xy$ -plane, moves so that two consecutive vertices
are always on the  $x$ -  and  $y$ -axes respectively. Find the locus of the midpoint of the square.
solution_md:
$\emph{Proof1.}$  It is evident that  $OBEA$  is a cyclic quadrilateral which in turn implies that  $\angle{EOA}=\angle{EBA}=45^{\circ}$   $OE$  is a straight line with slope  $45^{\circ}$  making with  $+$  ve  $x$  axis where length of  $OE$  would be the interval  $[\sqrt{2}a,2a]$ .
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- $\emph{Proof2.}$  consider  $A(a) , B(ib) , E(e)$  , where  $a,ib,e$  are complex numbers. clearly  $(a-e)e^{i \frac{\pi}{2}}=(e-ib) \implies e=(a+b)e^{i \frac{\pi}{4}}$  , now since side of square is  $2a$  , let  $\angle{BAO}=\theta \implies a=2acos\theta, b=2a\sin\theta \implies e=\sqrt{2a}\sin\left(\theta+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)e^{i \frac{\pi}{4}} \implies \arg(e)=45^{\circ}$  and  $|e| \in [\sqrt{2}a, 2a]$ .  $\blacksquare$

stem_md: If a polynomial  $f(x)$  is divided by  $(x-a)^{2} (x-b)$ , where  $a\ne b$ , derive a formula for the remainder.
solution_md:
we notice the fact that  $f(x)=(x-a)^2(x-b)J(x)+mx^2+nx+p$ we get that 
\begin{align} 
f(a)=ma^2+na+p
f(b)=mb^2+nb+p
f'(a)=2ma+n
\end{align}

so we observe that  $n=f'(a)-2ma$  and  $p=f'(a)-af'(a)+ma^2$ so formula for remainder is  $\boxed{mx^2+(f'(a)-2ma)x+f(a)-af'(a)+ma^2}$  where

  $m=\frac{(a-b)f'(a)-(f(a)+f(b))}{(a-b)^2}$

stem_md: Is the series   $$ \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{n!}{(n+1)^{n}}\cdot \left(\frac{19}{7}\right)^{n} $$  convergent or divergent?
solution_md:
ratio test due to Jean le Rond d'Alembert says that if  $x_n$  is a non zero sequence in  $\mathbb{R}$  and suppose the limit  $r=\lim\left|\frac{x_{n+1}}{x_n}\right|$  exists and  $r<1,$  then  $\sum x_n$  is absolutely convergent.

so just doing the same thing with the following thing and after some algebraic steps we reach here  $r=\frac{19}{7}\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{n+1}{n+2}\right)^{n+1}$ now some limit computations  $\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{n+2}{n+1}\right)^{n+1}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1+\frac{1}{n+1}\right)^{n+1}=e$ and since  $r=\frac{19}{7e}<1$  (use calculator if allowed  :)) and hence the series is convergent.  $\blacksquare$ **edit:**if you don't want to use calculator the only other method is to know the value of  $e$  which is close to  $2.718\cdots$  and just carry out the division.

stem_md: Find the orthogonal trajectories of the family of conics  $(x+2y)^{2} = a(x+y)$ . At what angle do the curves of one family cut the curves of the other family at the origin?
solution_md:
Let's do one of the oldies. Taking derivatives we find  $2(x+2y)(1+2y')=a(1+y')={{(x+2y)^2 (1+y')}\over {x+y}}$  and rewriting gives  $y'={{-x}\over {3x+2y}}$ . For the orthogonal field we have  $y'=2y/x+3$  with solution  $y=cx^2 -3x$ .
The first family has linear part  $x+y=0$  at the origin when  $a\not=0$  hence the tangent is  $y=-x$ . Except when  $a=0$ , then  $y=-x/2$ .
The second family has a common derivative -3 at the origin.

If  $a\not=0$  then the angle follows from  $\tan \phi={{3-1}\over {1+3\cdot 1}}=1/2$ . 
If  $a=0$  then the angle follows from  $\tan \phi={{3-1/2}\over {1+3/2}}=1$ , hence  $\phi=\pi/4$ .

stem_md:
A square of side  $2a$ , lying always in the first quadrant of the  $xy$ -plane, moves so that two consecutive vertices
are always on the  $x$ - and  $y$ -axes respectively. Prove that a point within or on the boundary of the square will in general describe a portion of a conic. For what points of the square does this locus degenerate?
solution_md:
Let  $A$  be the vertex that moves along the  $x-$ axis and  $B$  the vertex that moves along the  $y-$ axis. Suppose that when  $AB$  is horizontal, a point  $P$  has coordinates  $b, c$ . In the general configuration let  $\angle{ BAO} = \theta$  (where  $O$  is the origin). Then  $P$  has coordinates: $x = (2a - b) \cdot cos \theta + c \cdot sin \theta, y = b \cdot sin \theta + c \cdot cos \theta$ . 

Hence  $cx - (2a - b)y = (b^2 + c^2 - 2ab)sin \theta$ , and  $bx - cy = (2ab - b^2 - c^2)cos \theta$ . Squaring and adding we eliminate  $\theta$  to get:  $(b^2 + c^2)x^2 - 4acxy + (4a^2 + b^2 + c^2 - 4ab)y^2 = (b^2 + c^2 - 2ab)^2$ ;

which is the equation of a conic. So the locus of  $P$  must form part of this conic.

The conic degenerates if  $b^2 + c^2 = 2ab$ . In this case, the equation becomes: $2ab ^2 - 4acxy + (4a^2 - 2ab)y^2 = 0 \Rightarrow bx^2 - 2cxy + (2a - b)y^2 = 0 \Rightarrow b^2x^2 - 2bcxy + c^2y^2 = 0 \Rightarrow bx = cy$ . 

So in this case, the locus lies on a straight line. We may write the condition  $b^2 + c^2 = 2ab$  as  $(a - b)^2 + c^2 = a^2$ , which shows that such points  $P$  lie on the semicircle with diameter  $AB$ .

stem_md: A particle moves under a central force inversely proportional to the  $k$ -th power of the distance. If the particle describes a circle ( the central force proceeding from a point on the circumference of the circle ), find  $k$ .
solution_md:
The equations of motion are  $r (\theta')^{2} - r'' = \frac{a}{r^k}, r^{2}\theta' = A$  (due to conservation of angular momentum).

If the particle moves in a circle as described, then we can write its orbit as  $r = B\cos(\theta)$ . Differentiating,  $r' = - B\theta' \sin(\theta) = -\frac{AB}{r^2} \sin(\theta)$ . Differentiating again yields:  $r'' = -AB\cos(\theta) \cdot \frac{A}{r^2} + \frac{2AB}{r^3}\sin(\theta) r' = -\frac{A^2}{r^3} - \frac{2A^{2}B^{2}}{r^5}\sin(2\theta) = -\frac{A^2}{r^3} - \frac{2A^{2}B^{2}}{r^5} (1 - r^{2}B^{2}) = \frac{A^2}{r^3} - \frac{2A^{2}B^{2}}{r^5}$ . 

Substituting back in the equation of motion we get:  $\frac{2A^{2}B^{2}}{r^5} = \frac{a}{r^k}$ . Hence,  $\textcolor{red}{k = 5}$ .

stem_md: If  $a(x), b(x), c(x)$  and  $d(x)$  are polynomials in  $ x$ , show that  $$  \int_{1}^{x} a(x) c(x)\; dx\; \cdot \int_{1}^{x} b(x) d(x) \; dx -  \int_{1}^{x} a(x) d(x)\; dx\; \cdot \int_{1}^{x} b(x) c(x)\; dx $$  is divisible by  $(x-1)^4.$
solution_md:
$f(x)= \int_{1}^{x} a(x) c(x)\; dx\; \cdot \int_{1}^{x} b(x) d(x) \; dx -  \int_{1}^{x} a(x) d(x)\; dx\; \cdot \int_{1}^{x} b(x) c(x)\; dx$ since  $(x-1)^4$  divides  $f(x),$  it will have have the same root  $1$  with multiplicity  $4$  and hence we should have  $f(1)=f'(1)=f''(1)=f'''(1)=0$ <details><summary>note</summary>for brevity i will write the polynomials as  $a,b,c,d$  and to avoid confusion i will replace  $dx$  with  $dt$  and for calculating derivative i will be making use of leibnitz rule and product rule.</details> $f(1)=0$   $$ f'(x)=ac\int_1^x (bd)dt+bd\int_1^x (ac)dt-ad\int_1^x (bc)dt-bc\int_1^x (ad)dt, $$  again  $f'(1)=0$   $$ f''(x)=(ac)'\int_1^x (bd)dt+abcd+(bd)'\int_1^x (ac)dt+abcd-(ad)'\int_1^x (bc)dt-abcd-bc\int_1^x (ad)dt-abcd $$    $$ =(ac)'\int_1^x (bd)dt+(bd)'\int_1^x (ac)dt-(ad)'\int_1^x (bc)dt-(bc)'\int_1^x (ad)dt $$   
again  $f''(1)=0$   $$ f'''(x)=(ac)''\int_1^x (bd)dt+(ac)'bd+(bd)''\int_1^x (ac)dt+(bd)'ac-(ad)''\int_1^x (bc)dt-(ad)''\int_1^x (bc)dt-(ad)'bc-(bc)''\int_1^x (ad)dt-(bc)'ad $$    
now expanding like these  $(ac)'bd$  bit more by product rule we see that again  $f'''(1)=0\blacksquare$

stem_md: Find the smallest volume bounded by the coordinate planes and  by a tangent plane to the ellipsoid  $$ \frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}+\frac{z^{2}}{c^{2}}=1. $$
solution_md:
Consider WLOG then the first octant and  $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$  a point of the ellipsoid

The equation of the tangent plane is easy to proof, but I left to you. its  $\frac{x_0x}{a^2}+\frac{y_0y}{b^2}+\frac{z_0z}{c^2}=1$ The plane cuts in the three axis  $x,y,z$  in  $x=a^2/x_0$ ,  $y=b^2/y_0$  and  $z=c^2/z_0$ . Therefore it forms a pyramid with height  $c^2/z_0$  and base a right triangle with sides  $a^2/x_0$  and  $b^2/y_0$ , so the volume is  $\frac{a^2b^2c^2}{6x_0y_0z_0}$ . We conclude noting that by AM-GM: $\frac{x_0y_0z_0}{abc}\leq (\frac{\frac{x_0^2}{a^2}+\frac{y_0^2}{b^2}+\frac{z_0^2}{c^2}}{3})^{3/2}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}$  with equality in  $x_0/a=y_0/b=z_0/c=1/\sqrt{3}$ So  $V=\frac{a^2b^2c^2}{6x_0y_0z_0}=\frac{abc}{6}\frac{abc}{x_0y_0z_0}\geq \frac{3\sqrt{3} abc}{6}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}abc$ . therefore the minimum volume is  $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}abc$  attained in the points  $(x_0,y_0,z_0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(a,b,c)$ . 

The extension is quite evident by putting signs in each coordinate.

stem_md: For each positive integer  $n$ , put   $$ p_n =\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right)^{n},\; P_n =\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right)^{n+1}, \; h_n = \frac{2 p_n P_{n}}{ p_n + P_n }. $$  Prove that  $h_1 < h_2 < h_3 <\ldots$
solution_md:
$h_n=\frac{2\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right)^{2n+1}}{\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right)^{n}\left(2+\frac{1}{n}\right)}=\frac{2(n+1)^{n+1}}{n^n(2n+1)}$ we extend the function from  $\mathbb{N}$  to  $\mathbb{R_+}$ consider  $f(x)=\ln2 + (x+1)\ln(x+1)-x\ln(x)-\ln(2x+1)$  $f'(x)=\ln\left(\frac{x+1}{x}\right)-\frac{2}{2x+1}$   $f''(x)=-\frac{1}{x(x+1)(2x+1)}<0\quad\forall x>0$ which means that  $f'(x)$  is a decreasing function but also observe that  $\lim_{x\to\infty}=0$  hence the function is bounded below by  $0,$  that means  $f'(x)>0\quad\text{on}\quad x>0$  hence  $f(x)$  is increasing.

since  $f(x)$  is increasing so will  $e^{f(x)}$ .

since we proved for the stronger case of reals, it will also be true for  $n\in\mathbb{N}$  and hence  $h_1 < h_2 < h_3 <\ldots\blacksquare$

stem_md: In a solid sphere of radius  $R$  the density  $\rho$  is a function of  $r$ , the distance from the center of the sphere. If the magnitude of the gravitational force of attraction due to the sphere at any point inside the sphere is  $k r^2$ , where  $k$  is a constant, find  $\rho$  as a function of  $r.$  Find also the magnitude of the force of attraction at a point outside the sphere at a distance  $r$  from the center.
solution_md:
A shell exerts no net attraction on a point inside and acts on a point outside as if all its mass was concentrated at its center. So let the density at a radial distance  $r$  be  $\rho(r)$ . Then  $\frac{G}{r^2} \int_{0}^{r} 4\pi t^2\rho(t) dt = kr^2$ . Hence  $\int_{0}^{r} t^2\rho(t) dt = \frac{kr^4}{4G\pi}$ . Differentiating:  $r^2\rho(r) = \frac{kr^3}{G\pi}$ . So  $\rho(r) = \frac{kr}{G\pi}$ .

The force at the surface of the sphere  $(R)$  is  $kR^2$ . Hence the force at a distance  $r > R$  from the center of the sphere is  $\textcolor{red}{\frac{kR^4}{r^2}}$ . 

NOTE: The force is a simple inverse square law outside the sphere and it must be continuous at the surface.

stem_md: Show that  $\lceil (\sqrt{3}+1)^{2n})\rceil$  is divisible by  $2^{n+1}.$
solution_md:
what we essentially want to prove is that the integer next to  $(\sqrt{3}+1)^{2n}$  should be divisible by  $2^{n+1}$ claim  $\lceil (\sqrt{3}+1)^{2n})\rceil=(\sqrt{3}+1)^{2n}+(\sqrt{3}-1)^{2n}$ let  $(\sqrt{3}+1)^{2n}=a_n+\sqrt{3}b_n$ and  $(\sqrt{3}-1)^{2n}=a_n-\sqrt{3}b_n$ adding both of these we get  $(\sqrt{3}+1)^{2n}+(\sqrt{3}-1)^{2n}=2a_n$ observe  $\sqrt{3}-1<1$  raise it to any power  $n\ge1$  and it will be less than one, hence indeed  $\lceil (\sqrt{3}+1)^{2n})\rceil=(\sqrt{3}+1)^{2n}+(\sqrt{3}-1)^{2n}$ now we only have to prove that  $2^n|a_n$ we claim that  $2^n$  divides both  $a_n$  as well as  $b_n.$ proof: by induction

base case  $n=1$  is trivially true  $a_n=4,\quad b_n=2$ sps the claim is true for  $n=k$  now for  $n=k+1$  we get that  $a_{k+1}+\sqrt{3}b_{k+1}=(a_k+b_k)(1+\sqrt{3})^2=(4+2\sqrt{3})(a_k+\sqrt{3}b_k)=(4a_k+6b_k)+(4b_k+2a_k)\sqrt{3}$ hence  $a_k=2(a_k+3b_k)\quad\text{and}\quad b_k=1(a_k+2b_k)$  and by induction hypothesis our proof is complete. $\blacksquare$

Moreover, if $a_n<1$  for some  $n$ , then  $a_{n+1} \in (0,1)$  and hence  $a_m \in (0,1)$  for all  $m>n$ .
On the other hand, if  $a_n>1$  for all  $n$ , then  $a_n \in (1,2)$  for all  $n$ .
In both cases  $a_n \in (0,2)$  for all large  $n$ . But under that assumption, we see that  $(a_n-1)^2 \ge 0$  and hence  $a_n(2-a_n) \le 1$  and hence  $a_{n+1} \ge a_n$  i.e. the sequence is eventually monotonically increasing, but also bounded, hence convergent, say to  $\alpha \in [0,2]$ .
But then  $(\alpha-1)^2=0$  and hence  $\alpha=1$  as desired.

Note that if  $a_n=\frac{x}{y}$  then  $a_{n+1}=\frac{1}{2-\frac{x}{y}}=\frac{y}{2y-x}$ .

Therefore  $a_n=\frac{x_n}{y_n}$  where  $x_{n+1}=y_n$  and  $y_{n+1}=2y_n-x_n$  so that  $y_{n+1}=2y_n-y_{n-1}$  with characteristic equation  $\lambda^2=2\lambda-1$  having double root  $\lambda=1$ . So  $y_n=An+B$ .

So the general solution is  $a_n=\frac{A(n-1)+B}{An+B}=1-\frac{A}{An+B}$ , where  $A,B\in\mathbb{R}$  and not both zero. Clearly  $\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n=1$ .
